skill.name: When and where: clues to a story's time and place
skill.why: Knowing when and where a story happens helps everything else make sense.
skill.how: Spot clues in dates, objects, transport, weather and talk. Then add them up.

beats.say: The setting is when and where a story happens.
Writers often drop clues instead of telling you.
beats.show: The town had **no power lines yet**, so Ma lit the lamp.

beats.say: That's a clue to when. It's long ago.
Now hunt for clues to where.
beats.show: **Red dust** blew between **the tents of the goldfield**.

beats.say: Add them up. Long ago, at a goldfield.

weDo.success: Another planet. A station, a dome, two red moons and an oxygen tank all point there.

options.reason: Outside the glass there's dust and moons, not water.

creature.blurb: A shearwater that crosses whole oceans and never gets lost. It reads the clues around it to know exactly when and where it is.

encounters.text: Every morning, Kip's robot, Tumble, cooked pancakes, ironed his school shirt and flew him to school in a bubble-pod. Kip thought this was completely normal. But Grandma loved telling stories about 'the old days'. 'Back in the 2080s,' she would say, 'robots couldn't even cook! We had to make our own toast. With our hands!' Kip didn't believe her. 'And school was in a building on the ground,' she went on, 'not on the Moon.' Kip laughed so hard that he spilled his pancake juice. Tumble cleaned it up before it hit the floor. It was Kip's birthday on Friday. He was turning eleven, and Tumble had already planned the party at Moon Base Four.

encounters.text: Gannet Rock Lighthouse. Log kept by Edith Moore, aged twelve. 17 July 1894. The winter storms have not stopped for nine days, and the waves are breaking right over the rock. Father and I climbed the hundred and twelve steps to the lamp room at dusk, as we do every night. I trimmed the wicks while he wound the great clockwork that turns the light. Without it, ships would never see the rocks in the dark. The supply boat should have come from the mainland a week ago, but no boat could land in this weather. We are down to our last sack of potatoes and one tin of jam. The mainland is only a thin grey line across the water, and on stormy days we cannot see it at all. Mother says the boat will come when the sea is calm. Until then, I am teaching our goat, Captain, to shake hands. He is not a fast learner.

encounters.frame: Narra the Teller is telling the story of a famous race. The Wherrow is cheering for the blue chariot.
encounters.text: The Great Chariot Race of Korinthea began at noon, when the sun was directly overhead and the stone seats of the stadium were too hot to sit on. It was the third year of King Thalos's reign, and the whole city had come to watch. Twelve chariots lined up on the sandy track, each pulled by four horses. Daros, the youngest driver, was only fourteen. His chariot was painted blue, and his horses were the fastest in the hills outside the city walls. The trumpet sounded. Dust flew up in clouds. The crowd roared so loudly that the pigeons on the temple roof took off in fright. On the final lap, Daros overtook the king's own nephew, and his blue chariot crossed the line first. That evening, as the sun set over the harbour, Daros was given a crown of olive leaves and a bag of silver coins. His horses were given a whole sack of apples.

encounters.frame: Narra the Teller is telling the story of a very strange night. The Wherrow is trying not to laugh.
encounters.text: Gerald had been the night guard at the city museum for thirty years, and nothing ever happened. Every evening, after the last visitors had gone home and the big front doors were locked, he did his rounds with a torch. He said goodnight to the stuffed lion in its glass case. He checked the labels on the giant moth collection. He tapped the toe of the dinosaur skeleton for luck. Then, at ten past two in the morning, he heard something crunching in the Hall of Birds. Gerald crept closer, his torch shaking. The crunching grew louder. A glass case stood open, and its little brass label lay on the floor: BRUSH-TURKEY. Gerald gulped. Then he shone his torch under a bench and found a very much alive brush-turkey, which had wandered in through a broken window. It was eating the wax fruit from the display. 'You're not even stuffed,' Gerald whispered. The turkey looked at him and kept crunching.

encounters.text: From the journal of Second Mate Amos Pike. Day 3. I am writing this by the light of a lantern I managed to keep dry, and I must tell you plainly where I am. On Tuesday, something enormous and grey rose beneath our rowboat, with a mouth as wide as a barn door, and the world went dark. The walls around me are pink, squishy and warm, and they gurgle like a giant tummy. Every few minutes, a rush of seawater pours in, bringing fresh fish, crabs and seaweed. The smell is beyond describing, though I will try: imagine a hundred old prawns left in the sun, then add socks. I have made a small camp on a slippery ledge and built a table out of a crate that was swallowed before me. Yesterday, a startled octopus joined me, and we have agreed to share the lantern. Tomorrow I plan to tickle the walls, in the hope that the whale will sneeze me out.

encounters.text: Aboard Hartley's Circus Train, somewhere on the great treeless plain. Tuesday, 9 April 1929. Dearest Gran, I am writing this with my notebook balanced on a crate of juggling clubs, so please forgive the wobbly letters. We have been rolling across the plain for two whole days now, and there has not been a single town or tree in all that time, only red earth and saltbush as far as I can see. The elephants ride in the last carriage, and every time the train goes over a bump, Duchess trumpets so loudly that the lions start roaring back. I practise my cornet for the circus band in the dining car each afternoon, though the drummer says I sound like a goose with a cold. Father sends you a telegram from every siding where the train stops to take on water, so you will probably know all our news before this letter arrives. Mother has sewn me a new costume with silver stars on it, ready for the next show. Our last show was in a big seaside city, and the crowds were enormous. The next one is still four days away, at the end of the line, and I shall post this when we get there. Your loving granddaughter, Clara.

encounters.frame: Indi found a story about a mural painted far in the future. The Wherrow loves the whale.
encounters.text: Sol had been planning the mural for months. In the winter of 2140, the council of Neo Harbour finally gave her permission to paint the blank wall of the sky-tram station, forty storeys above the sea. Neo Harbour floats; it has floated ever since the old coastline disappeared under the water, and on windy days the whole city rocks gently, like a ship at anchor. Sol started work just before dawn, when the sky-trams were still parked and the platforms were empty. She clipped her harness to the railing, switched on her hover-palette and began spraying the outline of an enormous whale. Purple was her favourite colour, so the whale was purple. Below her, a fishing drone buzzed past with a crate of mussels. By midday, a small crowd had gathered on the platform below, pointing and taking photos. A little boy asked if the whale was real. Sol told him that once, long ago, whales like that had swum right past the place where they were standing. She hummed while she worked, the same tune her grandmother used to hum. By evening, the whale was finished, its tail curling around the station clock, and the first night trams were sliding past it, their windows full of faces.

encounters.frame: Zed says this story happened to a friend of his. The Wherrow thinks Zed knows more than he's saying.
encounters.text: Kestrel woke up in a forest where every tree was exactly the same height. That was the first strange thing. Even the clouds moved in neat rows, as if they were waiting their turn. The second was the glowing green bar floating just above her head, which shrank a little every time she bumped into something. She walked to the edge of a river and found that the water didn't splash; it just shimmered, like a picture of water. A sign beside the path said SAVE POINT, and when she touched it, a cheerful chime rang out from nowhere. Further along, a frog hopped past her, stopped, hopped back the other way, and then did exactly the same thing again, over and over, as if it had forgotten how to do anything else. When she finally tripped over a root and fell into the river, everything went black. A moment later, she was standing beside the SAVE POINT sign again, completely dry, with her green bar full. High above the trees, in the top corner of the sky, a small white message flickered: PLAYER 2 HAS JOINED. Kestrel looked up and narrowed her eyes. Somewhere, she realised, someone was holding a controller, and she had a very good idea who it was.

encounters.frame: Mo found a letter from a boy who became famous for falling over. He wrote a note about it, but one word is wrong.
encounters.text: 2 August 1924. Dear Frank, You will never believe it, but I am going to be in the pictures! The studio needed a boy who could fall over in a funny way, and I have been falling over for years, so I got the job. The studio is a huge glass shed, so that plenty of sunlight can get in, because the camera needs lots of light. The camera is a big wooden box on three legs, and a man turns a handle on the side to make it film. Nobody in the audience will hear a single word we say, so the director shouts through a cone the whole time, and the actors pull enormous faces instead of talking. Afterwards, a lady writes what we are meant to be saying on little black cards, which will appear on the screen between the scenes. In my big scene, I get hit in the face with a custard pie. We did it eleven times. The custard was real, and by the end, so was my headache. The film will be shown at the Regent Picture Palace in October, with Mrs Hodge playing the piano in front of the screen. Mother says I must not let it go to my head. Father says it has already gone to my head and moved in. Please tell everyone. Your famous cousin, Bertie.

encounters.frame: The second tide brought in a letter sealed with black wax. The Wherrow is hiding behind Wren.
encounters.text: Blackwater Hall, 31 October 1893. Nearly midnight. My dear sister Lucy, I am writing by the light of a single candle in the nursery, with the door locked and a chair wedged under the handle, so you must forgive my shaking hand. The children are asleep at last, and Cook went to bed hours ago, so I am quite alone. The Hall is so large that the wind gets lost in its chimneys, and tonight a storm is rattling every window. Earlier this evening, as I walked through the long gallery with a tray of cocoa, I saw it: a tall white figure drifting between the portraits, moaning softly. I dropped the tray, cocoa and all, and ran back up the stairs without stopping. Now I can hear footsteps in the corridor outside, slow and shuffling, and a faint rustling, like paper. Wait. The footsteps have stopped outside my door. Someone is whispering. It sounds very much like Mr Grimsby, the butler, and he is asking whether anyone has seen the biscuit tin. Lucy, I believe our ghost may be a butler in a bedsheet with a weakness for shortbread. I shall find out in the morning. Your ever-loving sister, Agnes Penhallow.

encounters.success: In the nursery, near midnight. She ran there from the gallery and locked herself in to write.
